title: What is continuing professional development (CPD)?
description: Continuing professional development (CPD) is ongoing learning professionals must do to stay competent. How CPD, CPE and CLE differ, with examples.
shortAnswer: Continuing professional development (CPD) is the ongoing, structured learning that professionals undertake after qualifying to maintain, update and broaden the knowledge and skills their work requires. Professional bodies and regulators usually make it a condition of membership, registration or a practicing certificate, set minimum hours or units over a period, and audit records. Accountants in the United States call it continuing professional education (CPE) and lawyers call it continuing legal education (CLE).
keyTakeaways: CPD obligations are set by professional bodies and regulators, not general employment law, and are usually tied to keeping a license, registration or membership.
Requirements are typically expressed as hours or units over a cycle, sometimes with annual minimums and compulsory topics such as ethics.
CPD, CPE and CLE describe the same idea in different professions and markets; the rules behind each label differ.
The professional is responsible for meeting and recording CPD; employers often support it and may rely on it as evidence of competence.
Hours prove participation, not competence, so regulated employers usually pair CPD records with role specific assessment.

sections.heading: How do professional bodies define CPD?

blocks.text: Professional bodies define CPD by its purpose: keeping a practitioner competent throughout their career. The Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra) [describes CPD](https://www.ahpra.gov.au/Registration/Registration-Standards/CPD.aspx) as "how health practitioners maintain, improve and broaden their knowledge, expertise and competence, and develop the personal and professional qualities required throughout their professional lives," and states that practitioners engaged in any form of practice must participate regularly in CPD relevant to their scope of practice.

In United States accounting, the [Statement on Standards for Continuing Professional Education (CPE) Programs](https://www.nasbaregistry.org/the-standards), published jointly by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) and the National Association of State Boards of Accountancy (NASBA), states that CPE "is required for CPAs to maintain their professional competence and provide quality professional services." A revised edition of those standards took effect on August 1, 2026, with transition dates running to November 1, 2028 for existing programs.

sections.heading: What is the difference between CPD, CPE and CLE?

blocks.text: CPD, CPE and CLE all mean mandatory ongoing learning for qualified professionals; the label depends on the profession and market. The underlying rules, such as cycle length, units and audit, differ far more than the names do.

blocks.text: What counts depends on the body, but most accept a mix of structured learning, such as courses, seminars and postgraduate study, and some less formal activities, often with caps. The Law Society of NSW, for example, limits units for private study of audio or visual material, writing articles and committee work. Many bodies require the activity to be relevant to the professional's current or intended role, and some require it to be verifiable through a certificate or attendance record.

Requirements can also specify topics. CPA Australia sets a minimum for verifiable ethics learning, and the NSW solicitor rules require at least one unit in each of four compulsory fields. Professionals should check their own body's current rules; the examples here illustrate structure, not a universal standard.

sections.heading: Why does CPD matter to employers in regulated industries?

blocks.text: CPD keeps employed professionals eligible to practice, so a lapse can take a person out of a regulated role. Employers therefore track CPD status alongside their own [mandatory training](/glossary/mandatory-training), and many fund or deliver CPD eligible courses.

items: **Eligibility risk:** track renewal dates and cycle deadlines so lapses are seen before they happen.

**Evidence of competence:** CPD hours show participation in learning. They do not show the person can apply your procedures, so pair them with [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment) for critical tasks.
**Double use:** internal training on regulatory change can often count toward CPD if it meets the body's criteria, which reduces duplication.
**Records:** professionals usually keep their own CPD records for audit, but an employer's [learning record store](/glossary/learning-record-store) or LMS can provide supporting evidence.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps internal learning to the competencies and obligations it covers, which makes it easier to show which activities are relevant to a professional's role for CPD purposes. Assessment results sit alongside participation, so employers can show both learning hours and verified competence.

faqs.a: For many professions it is, either directly in legislation or through rules made by a regulator or professional body under statute. For example, CPD is a condition of registration for health practitioners regulated by Ahpra and of practicing certificates for NSW solicitors. For others it is a membership condition of a voluntary professional body.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for completing and recording CPD?
faqs.a: The individual professional, in almost every scheme. Employers may provide time, funding and training, but the professional declares compliance at renewal and must produce records if audited.

faqs.q: Does employer compliance training count toward CPD?
faqs.a: It can, if it meets the professional body's criteria for relevance, structure and verification. Many bodies accept employer delivered training. The professional should keep evidence such as a certificate of completion, learning outcomes and hours.

faqs.q: What happens if a professional does not meet CPD requirements?
faqs.a: Consequences vary: audit findings, conditions on registration, refusal to renew, inactive status, or loss of membership. Some schemes allow extensions or exemptions for illness, parental leave or not practicing. The specific body's rules set the outcome.
